content.title: Concrete Specifications
content.subtitle: The mix, the reinforcement and the base we use on every job — and why they matter in Ohio.

content.title: Specs You Can Ask About
content.paragraph1: Most concrete quotes look the same on paper. The difference shows up years later — in the cracks, the settling and the surface wear. What separates one driveway from another is the mix, the reinforcement and the base underneath it.
content.paragraph2: These are the specifications Maxima Concrete uses as standard on residential work. Bring them to any estimate you receive: if a contractor cannot tell you the bag count, the reinforcement and the base preparation, you are not comparing the same product.

content.title:
What We Pour, 
As Standard
content.description: Every residential pour leaves our team with the same build sheet. Key specifications:

items.text: A high-strength mix with 6.5 bags of cement per cubic yard, rated at 4500 PSI — well above the minimum used on budget work.
Structural fibers dispersed through the mix act like micro-rebar, controlling shrinkage cracks as the slab cures.
Steel mesh distributes load across the slab, preventing the large cracks and deformation that come from freeze-thaw movement.
A properly graded and compacted base carries the load and keeps water from washing out the ground under the slab.

content.title:
Built for 
Ohio Winters
content.description: Ohio puts concrete through dozens of freeze-thaw cycles every year. Water gets into the surface, freezes, expands and forces the slab apart from the inside. Everything in our build sheet exists to slow that down.

benefits.title: Drainage First
benefits.description: Grading moves water away from the slab and the foundation before it can pool or soak in.

benefits.title: Control Joints
benefits.description: Joints are cut where the slab is expected to move, so cracking happens on a straight line instead of at random.

benefits.title: Proper Curing
benefits.description: The slab is protected and monitored while it cures — strength comes from curing, not just from the mix.

benefits.title: Inspected Throughout
benefits.description: Base, reinforcement and finish are each checked before the crew moves on to the next stage.

items.question: What does "6.5-bag mix" mean?
items.answer: It refers to how many 94-lb bags of cement go into each cubic yard of concrete. More cement means higher compressive strength — our 6.5-bag mix is rated at 4500 PSI. Budget work often uses a leaner mix, which costs less and cracks sooner.

items.question: Do I need both fiber mesh and wire mesh?
items.answer: They solve different problems. Fiber mesh is mixed into the concrete and controls the fine shrinkage cracks that form while the slab cures. The 10-gauge wire mesh sits in the slab and holds it together across larger movements, like frost heave. We use both on residential flatwork.

items.question: How thick should the slab be?
items.answer: It depends on what the surface has to carry. Most residential basement floors are poured 3–4 inches thick, with additional reinforcement where extra durability is needed. Driveways and slabs that take vehicle or equipment loads are built heavier, and we size them during the estimate.

items.question: Why does the base matter as much as the concrete?
items.answer: Concrete is strong in compression but has very little tolerance for uneven support. If the ground under the slab settles or washes out, the slab bridges the gap and cracks — no matter how good the mix was. That is why the compacted gravel base is a specification and not an optional step.

items.question: Will my concrete crack?
items.answer: All concrete moves. The goal is to control where it cracks, not to promise it never will. Control joints, reinforcement and a stable base keep movement predictable and hairline instead of structural.
